phrase:
An owl and a pigeon lived in the same forest.
They practiced the language of the meadow birds together.

Every time the pigeon spoke, the owl reached into her coat.
She unrolled a small grammar chart.

"Actually," the owl said,
"the correct form is the third conjugation."

One morning the pigeon flew to the meadow.
He ordered seeds from a sparrow.

He used the wrong word.
The sparrow laughed, understood, and gave him the seeds.

The owl arrived moments later.
The chart already unrolled.

"You said it incorrectly."
"The sparrow still gave me the seeds," said the pigeon.

The pigeon made the same mistake the next day.
And the day after.

Each time, someone understood him.
Each time, the owl corrected him.

One afternoon the pigeon said the wrong word again.
Three birds laughed. And stayed to talk for an hour.

The owl stood at the edge of the group.
Chart in hand. Waiting.
She put the chart back in her coat.

Said something.
Slightly wrong.
And stayed.
